**[III. Dalton Creek Disposal Facility --- CERCLA Exposure]{.underline}**

**[A. Background]{.underline}**

Cascadia formerly operated at the Dalton Creek disposal facility, a former hazardous waste disposal site located in Clackamas County, Oregon. The Company\'s operations at Dalton Creek involved the handling, treatment, and disposal of hazardous wastes generated by third-party industrial customers. These operations significantly predate the current management team and were conducted during a period when the Company was under different operational leadership. According to records produced during due diligence and confirmed by management interviews, Cascadia ceased all operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility in approximately 2015.

In February 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 10, issued an information request to Cascadia under Section 104(e) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, as amended (\"CERCLA\"), 42 U.S.C. § 9604(e). The information request seeks comprehensive documentation of the Company\'s waste handling and disposal activities at the Dalton Creek facility, including waste manifests, disposal records, volume and characterization data, and operational history during the period of the Company\'s use of the site.

As of the date of this memorandum, no formal enforcement action, notice of potential responsible party (\"PRP\") designation, unilateral administrative order, or lawsuit has been filed or issued by EPA or any other party against Cascadia in connection with the Dalton Creek facility. However, the issuance of a § 104(e) information request is widely recognized as a standard precursor to potential PRP designation and subsequent enforcement activity under CERCLA. The Company\'s management confirmed that it has retained outside environmental counsel to assist with the response to the information request and to monitor developments at the site.

**[B. Estimated Liability Exposure]{.underline}**

Based on our review of the Company\'s records, the EPA information request and the Company\'s response, publicly available site information, and consultation with environmental counsel experienced in CERCLA cost allocation proceedings, we estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in connection with the Dalton Creek disposal facility to be in the range of **\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000**. The factors underlying this range are as follows:

> • **Low End (\$1,500,000).** This estimate assumes that EPA pursues a multi-party cost allocation among all identified potentially responsible parties at the Dalton Creek site, that Cascadia\'s proportionate share of total cleanup costs is determined on the basis of the volume and toxicity of waste it disposed at the facility, and that other identified PRPs remain solvent and capable of bearing their respective shares. Under this scenario, Cascadia\'s share would represent a minority allocation consistent with its relative contribution to site contamination.
>
> • **High End (\$6,000,000).** This estimate reflects the possibility that EPA may designate Cascadia as a major contributor to the contamination at the site, or that one or more other PRPs may prove financially unable to satisfy their allocated shares. Under CERCLA § 107, liability is joint and several, meaning that EPA may seek recovery of the full cost of remediation from any single PRP, regardless of that party\'s proportionate contribution. If other PRPs are insolvent or unidentifiable, Cascadia\'s exposure could increase significantly. The high-end estimate also accounts for the possibility that the overall scope and cost of site remediation may exceed current projections.

It is important to note that CERCLA proceedings frequently extend over many years. Under CERCLA § 113(g)(2), the statute of limitations for a cost recovery action is six years from the date of completion of a remedial action at the site. Contribution claims under § 113(f) may extend further depending on the timing of settlement or judgment. Given that no formal remedial action has been initiated at the Dalton Creek site, it is possible that Cascadia\'s ultimate liability will not be determined for a period of years following the closing of the proposed transaction.

The Company\'s environmental impairment liability insurance with Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. (aggregate limit \$15,000,000; per-occurrence limit \$5,000,000) may provide coverage for defense costs and some portion of the Company\'s ultimate liability in connection with the Dalton Creek matter. However, coverage for legacy disposal operations is commonly subject to policy exclusions, including prior-knowledge exclusions, pollution date restrictions, and exclusions for known or disclosed conditions. We recommend that insurance counsel conduct a detailed review of the applicable policy terms to determine the extent and reliability of available coverage.

**[C. SPA Recommendations --- Dalton Creek]{.underline}**

Based on the foregoing analysis, we make the following recommendations with respect to the treatment of the Dalton Creek CERCLA exposure in the Stock Purchase Agreement:

**Recommendation 1 --- Special Indemnity.** Given the magnitude of the potential exposure (\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000), the fact that this is a known and disclosed environmental liability arising from Seller\'s period of ownership, and the inherent uncertainty and protracted timeline of CERCLA proceedings, we **strongly recommend** that the SPA include a **Special Indemnity** obligating Seller to indemnify Buyer for all Losses arising from or related to the Dalton Creek disposal facility and the EPA\'s CERCLA § 104(e) information request, including without limitation all costs of investigation, remediation, defense, settlement, contribution, and related administrative proceedings. The Special Indemnity should be structured as follows:

> \(a\) **Survival Period.** The Special Indemnity should survive for no less than **72 months** following the closing date, in order to account for the characteristically lengthy timeline of CERCLA proceedings and the six-year statute of limitations for CERCLA cost recovery actions under § 113(g)(2). A shorter survival period would create an unacceptable risk that Buyer\'s indemnification rights expire before a formal CERCLA claim crystallizes.
>
> \(b\) **Exclusion from General Basket and Cap.** The Special Indemnity should **not** be subject to the general indemnification deductible basket or aggregate liability cap. The Dalton Creek matter is a known, quantifiable exposure that should be indemnified on a dollar-for-dollar basis from the first dollar of Loss. Subjecting this exposure to general basket and cap limitations would improperly shift a portion of the known risk to Buyer.
>
> \(c\) **Escrow Holdback.** The Special Indemnity should be supported by a dedicated portion of the **escrow holdback** maintained with Pinnacle Trust Company for a minimum period of **36 months** following closing. The escrowed amount should be sufficient to cover at least the low end of the estimated liability range (\$1,500,000), with the full Special Indemnity obligation surviving for the 72-month period regardless of the release of escrowed funds.
>
> \(d\) **Consistency with Term Sheet.** We note that the executed term sheet dated September 10, 2025, between Whitmore Capital Partners LLC and Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc., specifically provides for a \"Special Indemnity\" to address the Dalton Creek matter. The SPA must implement this agreed-upon commercial term. Omission of the Special Indemnity from the Seller\'s initial SPA draft would represent a departure from the agreed deal terms.

**Recommendation 2 --- Extended Survival of Environmental Representations.** Independent of and in addition to the Dalton Creek Special Indemnity, the environmental representations and warranties in the SPA should survive for a minimum of **36 months** post-closing, and ideally for the **full applicable statute of limitations** for environmental claims. We understand that seller-favorable first drafts in the middle market typically propose a 12-month survival period for representations and warranties, including environmental representations. For a company whose core business is the provision of environmental remediation and hazardous waste management services, a 12-month survival period for environmental representations would be wholly inadequate for the following reasons:

> \(a\) The Dalton Creek CERCLA exposure may not crystallize into a formal claim, enforcement action, or PRP designation for a period of years following closing, as discussed in Section III.B above.
>
> \(b\) Cascadia\'s active remediation projects, including the Hargrove Industrial Site project, have multi-year performance timelines during which new environmental liabilities or breaches of environmental representations may emerge.
>
> \(c\) Environmental liabilities in the remediation services sector routinely emerge well beyond a 12-month period due to the nature of contamination migration, delayed regulatory action, and evolving site characterization data.
>
> \(d\) For a company whose entire value proposition is built upon environmental compliance and permitting, the environmental representations are among the most critical representations in the agreement and should be afforded extended protection commensurate with that importance.

We recommend that the deal team take a firm position on extended survival of environmental representations during SPA negotiations.

**[IV. Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation]{.underline}**

**[A. Project Overview]{.underline}**

Cascadia is currently performing active environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site, located in Milwaukie, Oregon, under a remediation services contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (\"Oregon DEQ\"). The Hargrove project involves soil and groundwater remediation activities at the former industrial site, including excavation and off-site disposal of contaminated soil, installation and operation of a groundwater extraction and treatment system, and ongoing environmental monitoring. The Company estimates the total remaining cost to complete the remediation at approximately **\$4,200,000**, with the project expected to continue for approximately 18 to 24 months beyond the anticipated closing date. The Hargrove remediation contract is one of the Company\'s four active government contracts and represents a significant ongoing commitment of Company resources and personnel.

**[B. Insurance Coverage]{.underline}**

Cascadia carries a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy issued by **Northshore Specialty Insurance Co.** with a **\$10,000,000 policy limit** specifically covering the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project. This policy provides coverage for remediation costs, cost overruns, and third-party claims arising from the Company\'s remediation activities at the Hargrove site. Separately, the Company\'s broader environmental impairment liability insurance with Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. carries an aggregate limit of \$15,000,000 and a per-occurrence limit of \$5,000,000. The site-specific Hargrove policy appears adequate to cover the estimated remaining \$4,200,000 remediation cost plus potential cost overruns and third-party claims, assuming no policy exclusions or coverage defenses are applicable. We recommend that the SPA include a representation that all environmental insurance policies maintained by the Company are in full force and effect, that all premiums due have been paid, and that no notice of cancellation, non-renewal, or material modification has been received. The SPA should also include a pre-closing covenant requiring the Company to maintain all such policies through and following the closing date.

**[C. Risk Assessment]{.underline}**

We assess the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project as a **moderate risk** item. The project is a standard remediation engagement being performed under a government contract with the Oregon DEQ. The principal risks are (i) cost overruns in excess of the current \$4,200,000 estimate, (ii) potential regulatory enforcement action if the Company fails to meet remediation milestones established in the work plan and consent order, and (iii) third-party claims arising from remediation activities. The available insurance coverage appears adequate to mitigate these risks. We note that the Oregon DEQ contract under which the Hargrove work is being performed is one of the four government contracts requiring novation or consent analysis, as discussed in Section VI below.

**[V. Environmental Permit Portfolio]{.underline}**

**[A. Overview of Permits]{.underline}**

Cascadia holds **23 active environmental remediation permits** across four states: Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada. The permit portfolio includes the following categories:

> • **RCRA Permits.** Treatment, storage, and disposal (TSD) facility permits issued under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act and corresponding state programs, authorizing the Company to handle, treat, store, and dispose of hazardous wastes at specified locations.
>
> • **Clean Water Act Discharge Permits.** National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits authorizing the Company to discharge treated water and stormwater from remediation project sites in compliance with applicable effluent limitations.
>
> • **Clean Air Act Emissions Permits.** Permits authorizing air emissions from remediation equipment, thermal treatment units, and related operations at Company facilities and project sites.
>
> • **State Hazardous Waste Transporter Permits.** Permits issued by state environmental agencies authorizing the Company to transport hazardous waste within and between states.
>
> • **State Remediation Contractor Licenses and Permits.** State-specific licenses and permits required to perform environmental remediation and hazardous waste management services as a licensed contractor.

All 23 permits are held in the name of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. In addition, 12 of the Company\'s employees hold professional engineer (\"PE\") licenses that are critical to maintaining permit compliance and performing permitted activities. Several of the Company\'s permits are conditioned upon the availability of a PE-licensed professional to oversee permitted operations. Loss of these PE-licensed employees, whether through attrition, termination, or failure to transfer to the post-closing entity, could jeopardize the Company\'s standing under certain permits and impair its ability to perform permitted work.

**[B. Change-of-Control Transfer and Notification Requirements]{.underline}**

Although this transaction is structured as a **stock purchase** --- and therefore the legal entity holding the permits (Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc.) will not change --- many state environmental regulatory programs nonetheless require **notification to or approval from the issuing agency** upon a change in the ownership or control of the permit holder. This is a critical issue that must be addressed in the SPA. The applicable state-specific requirements include:

> • **Oregon.** Oregon DEQ regulations require notification of a change of ownership or control of a permitted facility within 30 days of such change. Certain RCRA permits issued by Oregon DEQ may require formal transfer approval prior to the change taking effect. *See* OAR Chapter 340, Division 012 and applicable permit conditions.
>
> • **Washington.** The Washington Department of Ecology requires prior written notification for changes in control of permitted entities. Certain permits include conditions that expressly require agency approval of ownership changes before the transfer is deemed valid. *See* WAC Chapter 173-303 and applicable permit conditions.
>
> • **California.** The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (\"DTSC\") and regional water quality control boards often require notification and, in certain permit categories, prior approval for changes in control of entities holding hazardous waste facility permits and waste discharge requirements. The specific requirements vary by permit type and issuing authority.
>
> • **Nevada.** The Nevada Division of Environmental Protection requires notification of ownership changes for certain categories of environmental permits, including hazardous waste management permits and water pollution control permits.

Even in a stock acquisition, these agencies may treat a change of the ultimate parent company --- here, the acquisition of Cascadia\'s shares by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC from Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc. --- as a \"change of ownership or control\" that triggers notification or approval requirements under the applicable permit or regulation. Failure to comply with these requirements could result in permit violations, enforcement actions, fines, or in extreme cases, permit revocation or suspension. Given that Cascadia\'s business is entirely dependent upon its ability to perform work under these permits, any disruption to the permit portfolio would be material.

We anticipate that the Seller\'s SPA draft, once circulated, will include representations that all necessary environmental permits are held by the Company and are in good standing. However, a mere representation regarding the current status of permits is insufficient to protect Buyer from the risks associated with the change-of-control process. **[VI. Government Contract Regulatory Requirements]{.underline}**

**[A. Overview of Government Contracts]{.underline}**

Cascadia is party to **four active government contracts**, each of which is material to the Company\'s operations and revenue:

> 1\. **Oregon Department of Environmental Quality** --- Environmental remediation services, including the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project discussed in Section IV above.
>

>

>
> 4\. **Bureau of Land Management** --- Environmental site characterization and remediation services on federal lands managed by BLM.

These four government contracts collectively represent a material portion of Cascadia\'s annual revenue and serve as a foundation for the Company\'s ongoing business operations. Loss of any one or more of these contracts would have a material adverse effect on the Company\'s financial condition and business prospects.

**[B. Anti-Assignment Act and FAR Novation Requirements]{.underline}**

Federal government contracts are subject to the **Anti-Assignment Act, 41 U.S.C. § 6305**, which generally prohibits the transfer or assignment of government contracts without the consent of the contracting officer. While the Anti-Assignment Act has historically been interpreted to apply primarily to assignments of the contract itself (as opposed to changes in corporate ownership), the **Federal Acquisition Regulation (\"FAR\"), Part 42, Subpart 42.12**, specifically addresses changes in the contractor\'s organizational structure, including changes in ownership.

Under **FAR 42.1204**, when a contractor undergoes a change in ownership --- including when a third party acquires the stock of the contractor --- the contractor is required to submit a request for a **novation agreement** (or, in some cases, a **change-of-name agreement**) to the responsible contracting officer. A novation agreement formally recognizes the successor entity and transfers the government\'s contractual rights and obligations to the recognized successor. The key requirements under FAR 42.12 include:

> • **FAR 42.1204(a).** The contractor must submit a written request for novation to the responsible contracting officer, accompanied by supporting documentation including the acquisition agreement (or relevant portions thereof), a list of all affected contracts, and evidence of the transferee\'s technical and financial capability to perform.
>
> • **FAR 42.1204(e).** The contracting officer must make an affirmative determination that recognizing the successor is in the government\'s interest before executing the novation agreement.
>
> • **Interim Period.** Until a novation agreement is executed, the government may continue to treat the original contractor as the responsible party under the contract. Failure to obtain novation could result in the government treating the change of ownership as a breach of the contract, potentially leading to termination for default or termination for convenience.

**For the two federal contracts** --- the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contract and the Bureau of Land Management contract --- **novation agreements will be required** under FAR 42.12 because Whitmore Capital Partners LLC, a new parent entity with no prior relationship to Cascadia, is acquiring 100% of the outstanding stock of the Company from Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc.

**For the two state contracts** --- the Oregon DEQ contract and the Washington Department of Ecology contract --- analogous state procurement regulations may impose similar notification or approval requirements for changes in corporate ownership of a government contractor. The specific requirements depend on the terms of each contract and the applicable state procurement code. These state contracts require further review of their specific provisions and the relevant Oregon and Washington procurement regulations.

**Risk Assessment.** We assess this as a **HIGH RISK** item. Failure to obtain required novation agreements or government consents could result in **contract termination**, which would eliminate a material revenue stream, potentially trigger cross-default provisions under the Company\'s other contracts or financing arrangements, and materially impair the value of Buyer\'s investment. The novation process is not merely administrative --- contracting officers have discretion to deny novation if they determine that the successor entity does not have the capability or resources to perform, or if recognition is not in the government\'s interest.

**[C. SPA Recommendations --- Government Contracts]{.underline}**

Based on the foregoing analysis, we make the following recommendations:

**Recommendation 1 --- Pre-Closing Covenant.** The SPA should include a specific covenant requiring Seller and the Company to (a) promptly notify each government contracting officer (federal and state) of the contemplated transaction, (b) submit all required novation request packages under FAR 42.12 for the two federal contracts and all analogous submissions required under state procurement regulations for the two state contracts, and (c) use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain all required novation agreements, recognition agreements, or government consents prior to closing.

**Recommendation 2 --- Closing Condition or Specific Covenant.** The deal team should carefully consider whether to make completion of the government contract novation process a **condition to closing** or a **pre-closing best-efforts covenant with a post-closing cooperation tail**. Given that the FAR novation process can take 60 to 120 days or longer, requiring full novation completion as a hard closing condition could delay closing beyond the expected mid-January 2026 timeline or the February 28, 2026 outside date set forth in the term sheet. We recommend the following balanced approach:

> \(a\) Require that all novation requests and government notifications have been **submitted** to all relevant contracting officers prior to closing.
>
> \(b\) Require that no government contracting officer has **denied** a novation request or indicated an intent to terminate, suspend, or materially modify any government contract as a result of the contemplated transaction.
>
> \(c\) Include a **post-closing cooperation covenant** requiring Seller to continue cooperating in the novation process following closing, including executing documents, providing information, and participating in meetings with contracting officers as reasonably requested by Buyer.

**Recommendation 3 --- Representations.** The SPA should include specific representations that (a) Seller has provided complete and accurate copies of all government contracts, including all modifications, amendments, and task orders, (b) the Company is in material compliance with all terms of such government contracts, (c) no government contract is the subject of any pending or threatened termination, suspension, or debarment proceeding, and (d) to Seller\'s Knowledge, no contracting officer has indicated any intent to terminate, not renew, or materially modify any such contract.

**Recommendation 4 --- Risk Allocation.** If any government contract is terminated as a result of the change of ownership and the failure to obtain the required novation agreement or government consent, the resulting Losses --- including lost revenue, contract penalties, and consequential damages --- should be allocated to Seller through the indemnification provisions of the SPA.

We note that the Seller\'s SPA draft should be carefully reviewed to determine whether the conditions-to-closing article addresses government contract consents separately from general third-party consents. It is common in seller-favorable first drafts to group government contract consents with general commercial consents --- this approach is insufficient given the unique federal regulatory framework applicable to government contracts and the heightened risk of contract termination. Government contract novation should be treated as a distinct and specifically addressed closing requirement.

al laws or regulations" from the MAE definition. The problem is obvious: Casc=
adia Environmental Solutions *is* an environmental services company. If the e=
ntire environmental services industry suffers a downturn, or if a major regul=
atory change fundamentally alters compliance economics, those are precisely t=
he risks that should constitute an MAE for this target. As drafted, these car=
ve-outs effectively gut the MAE closing condition.

Add a "disproportionate impact" qualifier to both carve-outs, consistent with=
 the playbook position. The exception should read along the lines of: "except=
 to the extent such changes disproportionately affect the Company relative to=
 other participants in the environmental services industry." This is non-nego=
tiable from Whitmore's perspective.

**2. Sandbagging Provision (Section 9.06) =E2=80=94 CRITICAL**

I noticed an express anti-sandbagging provision in Section 9.06 =E2=80=94 the=
 draft says Buyer cannot recover for any breach of which Buyer "had Knowledge=
 as of the Closing Date." This is a dealbreaker.

The playbook mandates a pro-sandbagging clause in every PE acquisition, and f=
or good reason. Whitmore has conducted extensive diligence and has identified=
 various issues =E2=80=94 including the Dalton Creek CERCLA matter =E2=80=94 =
and they cannot afford to have their indemnification rights cut off by virtue=
 of having done thorough diligence. The whole point of representations and wa=
rranties is allocation of risk regardless of Buyer's knowledge.

Replace the anti-sandbagging language with an affirmative pro-sandbagging pro=
vision stating that Buyer's right to indemnification is not limited or affect=
ed by any knowledge obtained by Buyer or its representatives at any time, whe=
ther before or after Closing, regardless of whether such knowledge relates to=
 a breach. Draft this tightly.

**3. Earnout Operational Covenants (Section 2.05) =E2=80=94 CRITICAL**

The earnout provision is a major concern. The Seller's draft includes languag=
e requiring Buyer to operate the Target's business "in a manner consistent wi=
th past practice and in good faith to maximize the Earnout Payment." This is =
an extremely aggressive seller position. It would effectively give Seller vet=
o power over Buyer's integration plans during the earnout period through Dece=
mber 31, 2026.

Whitmore is acquiring Cascadia as a platform investment =E2=80=94 they intend=
 to make operational improvements, potentially acquire bolt-on targets, and r=
estructure the business. An affirmative covenant to "maximize" the earnout wo=
uld create litigation risk on virtually any business decision.

Per the playbook, the only acceptable earnout covenant is a negative covenant=
: Buyer shall not take actions with the *primary purpose* of avoiding or redu=
cing the earnout payment. No affirmative operational obligations. Revise acco=
rdingly.

Also confirm the earnout financial mechanics match the term sheet: $25,000,00=
0 maximum earnout payment; $38,000,000 Adjusted EBITDA threshold for full pay=
ment; $32,000,000 floor for pro-rata payment; linear interpolation between $3=
2M and $38M (approximately $4,166,667 per $1,000,000 of EBITDA above $32,000,=
000); measurement period ending December 31, 2026. Flag any discrepancies.

**4. Government Contract Consents =E2=80=94 CRITICAL**

I reviewed the environmental DD memo and the government contract issue is not=
 addressed anywhere in the Seller's draft conditions to closing. Cascadia hol=
ds 4 active government contracts =E2=80=94 Oregon DEQ, Washington Ecology, US=
 Army Corps of Engineers, and Bureau of Land Management.

While this is a stock deal and the contracting entity (Cascadia Environmental=
 Solutions, Inc.) does not technically change, the federal Anti-Assignment Ac=
t (41 U.S.C. =C2=A7 6305) and FAR 42.12 require novation agreements when a go=
vernment contractor undergoes a change in ownership or control. A stock acqui=
sition resulting in a new parent entity generally triggers the novation requi=
rement under FAR 42.1204. Failure to obtain novation or recognition agreement=
s could give the government the right to terminate the contracts.

These contracts are likely material to the Target's revenue and backlog. Add:=
 (a) a pre-closing covenant requiring Seller and the Company to cooperate in =
filing novation/recognition requests with the relevant agencies; (b) represen=
tations regarding the government contracts and their assignment/novation requ=
irements; and (c) consider whether government contract novation should be a c=
losing condition or a pre-/post-closing covenant. Making it a hard closing co=
ndition is likely impractical given agency timelines, so a covenant with coop=
eration obligations and reasonable best efforts may be more appropriate =E2=
=80=94 but flag this for discussion with the client. I plan to raise the timi=
ng question with Marcus on Monday.

**ADDITIONAL ISSUES**

**5. Indemnification Cap (Indemnification Article) =E2=80=94 HIGH**

The indemnification article needs a hard scrub against the term sheet. I noti=
ced the general indemnification cap appears to be set at 20% of enterprise va=
lue ($43,000,000), but the term sheet clearly provides for a 12.5% cap ($26,8=
75,000). This is not a drafting gray area =E2=80=94 the term sheet is unambig=
uous. Redline this to 12.5% and include a comment citing the applicable secti=
on of the term sheet.

Also confirm the escrow mechanics: $16,125,000 (7.5% of the $215,000,000 ente=
rprise value) held with Pinnacle Trust Company, 18 months for general claims =
and 36 months for Fundamental Reps and Special Indemnities.

**6. Environmental Rep Survival Period =E2=80=94 HIGH**

The DD memo from the environmental group flagged the Dalton Creek CERCLA expo=
sure (potential liability of $1,500,000 to $6,000,000) and the active Hargrov=
e Industrial Site remediation ($4,200,000 remaining costs). A 12-month surviv=
al period for environmental reps is wholly inadequate for an environmental se=
rvices company. Extend environmental rep survival to a minimum of 36 months p=
er the playbook, and flag the option of seeking the full statute of limitatio=
ns period =E2=80=94 noting that CERCLA has no statute of limitations for gove=
rnment cost recovery actions. I want to discuss with Marcus whether to push f=
or the longer period.

**7. Special Indemnity for Dalton Creek =E2=80=94 HIGH**

Tied to the environmental survival issue. The term sheet specifically provide=
s for a "Special Indemnity" for the Dalton Creek disposal facility matter. Th=
e Seller's draft does not include any special indemnity =E2=80=94 it treats D=
alton Creek as a general rep matter only.

Draft a Special Indemnity provision: 72-month survival, not subject to the ba=
sket or general cap, with the escrow holdback available for 36 months for Spe=
cial Indemnity claims. The provision should cover all losses arising from or =
relating to the Dalton Creek disposal facility, including the pending EPA inf=
ormation request under CERCLA =C2=A7 104(e) and any resulting investigation, =
cleanup, or enforcement action.

**8. Interim Covenant =E2=80=94 Affiliate Transactions =E2=80=94 HIGH**

The interim operating covenants section is missing any restriction on affilia=
te transactions between Seller and the Company. Remember that the EBITDA adju=
stments include $1,600,000 of above-market rent paid by Cascadia to a Seller =
affiliate. Without a covenant restricting affiliate dealings during the inter=
im period, Seller could expand those arrangements or enter into new ones. The=
 playbook is clear: require Buyer's prior written consent for any new, amende=
d, or terminated transaction with Seller or Seller affiliates. Add this coven=
ant.

**9. Debt Payoff Mechanics =E2=80=94 HIGH**

The Seller's draft is vague on closing indebtedness repayment =E2=80=94 it sa=
ys indebtedness will be repaid "on or promptly following the Closing Date." T=
his doesn't work for Whitmore or for Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. (=
the $125M acquisition lender). The term sheet requires payoff letters from al=
l holders of Target indebtedness =E2=80=94 Cascade Mutual Bank ($28,000,000 s=
enior term loan), Pacific Lease Corp. ($9,800,000 equipment financing), and t=
he $4,500,000 subordinated seller note from Evergreen Holdings =E2=80=94 at l=
east 3 business days prior to closing, with wire instructions. All indebtedne=
ss must be repaid simultaneously at closing through the funds flow. Add payof=
f letter delivery as a closing condition and revise the payment mechanics acc=
ordingly.

**10. Environmental Permit Transfer Cooperation =E2=80=94 MEDIUM**

The DD memo identified that many state environmental permits in Oregon, Washi=
ngton, California, and Nevada require notification to or approval from the is=
suing agency upon a change of control, even in a stock deal where the permit-=

ental permits. The Seller's draft includes a representation that Target holds=
 all required permits but has no pre-closing or post-closing cooperation cove=
nant for permit transfers or notifications.

tifications and applications both before and after closing. Even in a stock t=
ransaction, state regulators often treat a change of ultimate beneficial owne=
rship as a trigger for notification. Oregon DEQ and Washington Ecology both h=
ave these requirements.

**11. R&W Insurance Subrogation Waiver =E2=80=94 MEDIUM**

Whitmore Capital is obtaining a representations and warranties insurance poli=
cy from Granite Ridge Underwriters. The term sheet acknowledges this and the =
playbook requires that the SPA include a waiver of the insurer's subrogation =
rights against Seller except in cases of fraud. The Seller's draft makes no m=

viding that any R&W Insurance policy obtained by Buyer or its affiliates shal=
l not provide the insurer with any subrogation rights against Seller or its a=
ffiliates, except in cases of Seller's fraud. This is standard in the current=
 market and Seller's counsel should expect it.

**12. Non-Competition Covenant Scope =E2=80=94 MEDIUM**

The non-compete in the Seller's draft is far too broad =E2=80=94 5 years, all=
 of the United States, "any business." The term sheet is explicit: 3 years po=
st-closing, limited to environmental remediation and hazardous waste manageme=
nt services, in Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada only. Evergreen Ho=
ldings Group has construction and timber operations that would be swept in by=
 the overbroad language, which is both commercially unreasonable and raises e=
nforceability concerns under applicable state law. Narrow to match the term s=
heet exactly.

e time marking these up:

\"**Indebtedness**\" means, with respect to any Person, without duplication, (a) all obligations for borrowed money, (b) all obligations evidenced by bonds, debentures, notes, or similar instruments, (c) all obligations under capital leases or financing leases (as determined in accordance with GAAP), (d) all obligations for the deferred purchase price of property or services (other than trade payables incurred in the ordinary course of business), (e) all obligations, contingent or otherwise, under letters of credit (including standby and commercial), to the extent drawn upon, (f) all guarantees of any of the foregoing obligations of another Person, (g) all net obligations under interest rate swap, cap, collar, or similar agreements, and (h) all accrued and unpaid interest, premiums, penalties, fees, expenses, and other amounts payable in connection with the prepayment or repayment of any of the foregoing, including breakage costs. **[COVENANTS]{.underline}**
**Section 6.01 Conduct of Business Prior to Closing**

**(a)** From the date of this Agreement until the Closing Date (or the earlier termination of this Agreement in accordance with Article VIII), except as (i) required by applicable Law, (ii) set forth on Schedule 6.01, or (iii) consented to in writing by Buyer (which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed), Seller shall cause the Company to:
> \(i\) conduct its business in the ordinary course of business consistent with past practice in all material respects;

> \(ii\) use commercially reasonable efforts to preserve intact its business organization, relationships with customers, suppliers, licensors, licensees, Governmental Authorities, and other Persons with whom the Company has material business relationships, and to retain its current officers, key employees, and other key personnel;
> \(iii\) maintain in full force and effect all insurance policies of the Company or replacement policies with comparable coverage on terms no less favorable in the aggregate; and
> \(iv\) maintain its books and records in accordance with past practice and in compliance with applicable Laws.

**(b)** Without limiting the generality of Section 6.01(a), from the date of this Agreement until the Closing Date (or the earlier termination of this Agreement in accordance with Article VIII), except as (i) required by applicable Law, (ii) set forth on Schedule 6.01, or (iii) consented to in writing by Buyer (which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed), Seller shall not permit the Company to:
> \(i\) amend, modify, or restate the articles of incorporation, bylaws, or other organizational documents of the Company;

> \(ii\) issue, sell, transfer, pledge, dispose of, grant, or authorize the issuance, sale, transfer, pledge, disposition, or grant of any shares of capital stock, or any options, warrants, convertible securities, or other rights to acquire any shares of capital stock, of the Company;

> \(iii\) declare, set aside, authorize, make, or pay any dividend or other distribution (whether in cash, stock, property, or otherwise) in respect of any shares of capital stock of the Company, or repurchase, redeem, or otherwise acquire any shares of capital stock of the Company;
> \(iv\) incur, assume, guarantee, or become liable for any Indebtedness in an amount in excess of \$250,000 individually or \$750,000 in the aggregate;

> \(v\) make any capital expenditures in excess of \$500,000 individually or \$1,500,000 in the aggregate, other than capital expenditures contemplated by the Company\'s approved capital expenditure budget previously provided to Buyer;

> \(vi\) enter into, materially amend, modify, terminate, waive any material rights under, or renew any Company Material Contract (other than renewals in the ordinary course of business on substantially similar terms);

> \(vii\) (A) hire or engage any employee or independent contractor with annual compensation in excess of \$150,000, (B) terminate (other than for cause) any employee with annual compensation in excess of \$150,000, or (C) increase the compensation or benefits of any employee or independent contractor (other than annual merit-based increases in the ordinary course of business consistent with past practice for employees earning less than \$150,000 per year);

> \(viii\) settle, compromise, or consent to the entry of judgment in any Action involving payments by or to the Company in excess of \$200,000 or that would impose any non-monetary obligation on the Company;
> \(ix\) change any method of accounting or accounting practice, principle, or policy, except as required by changes in GAAP or applicable Law;

> \(x\) make, change, or revoke any material Tax election, settle or compromise any material Tax claim, audit, or assessment, file any amended Tax Return, or enter into any agreement with a Governmental Authority with respect to Taxes;

> \(xi\) sell, lease, transfer, license, abandon, permit to lapse, or otherwise dispose of any material assets or properties of the Company (other than sales of inventory or obsolete equipment in the ordinary course of business);
> \(xii\) grant, create, incur, assume, or suffer to exist any Encumbrance on any material asset or property of the Company (other than Permitted Encumbrances); or
> \(xiii\) enter into any non-competition, non-solicitation, exclusive dealing, or similar restrictive covenant agreement.
**Section 6.02 Access to Information**

From the date of this Agreement until the Closing Date (or the earlier termination of this Agreement in accordance with Article VIII), Seller shall, and shall cause the Company and its officers, directors, employees, accountants, counsel, and other Representatives to, upon reasonable prior notice, afford Buyer and its Representatives reasonable access during normal business hours to the Company\'s properties, offices, plants, other facilities, books, records, contracts, documents, and personnel, and shall furnish to Buyer and its Representatives such additional financial, operating, and other information regarding the Company as Buyer may reasonably request; *provided* that (a) such access shall not unreasonably interfere with the normal operations of the Company, (b) such access shall be conducted in a manner that preserves the confidentiality of the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, (c) Seller shall not be required to grant access to, or furnish, any information the disclosure of which would (i) violate any applicable Law, (ii) jeopardize any attorney-client privilege or other legal privilege, or (iii) contravene any binding obligation of confidentiality, and (d) all information provided pursuant to this Section 6.02 shall be subject to the terms and conditions of the Confidentiality Agreement.
**Section 6.03 Confidentiality**

The Mutual Confidentiality Agreement, dated as of June 20, 2025, between Seller and Buyer (the \"Confidentiality Agreement\") shall continue in full force and effect in accordance with its terms, and the terms of the Confidentiality Agreement are hereby incorporated herein by reference. If this Agreement is terminated prior to the Closing, the Confidentiality Agreement shall survive such termination in accordance with its terms.
**Section 6.04 HSR Act Filings**

**(a)** Each of Buyer and Seller shall, as promptly as practicable (and in no event later than ten (10) Business Days after the date of this Agreement), file or cause to be filed with the United States Federal Trade Commission and the United States Department of Justice all notifications and other documents and information required to be filed under the HSR Act with respect to the transactions contemplated by this Agreement.

**(b)** Buyer and Seller shall each use their reasonable best efforts to (i) obtain early termination of the applicable waiting period under the HSR Act, (ii) comply at the earliest practicable date with any request for additional information and documentary material that may be issued under the HSR Act, (iii) cooperate with the other Party in connection with any filing under the HSR Act and in connection with resolving any investigation or other inquiry of any Governmental Authority under the HSR Act, and (iv) take all actions necessary, proper, or advisable to cause the expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period under the HSR Act as promptly as practicable.
**(c)** Buyer shall pay all filing fees payable under the HSR Act in connection with the transactions contemplated by this Agreement.

**(d)** Each Party shall promptly notify the other Party of any substantive communication with, and any inquiry from, any Governmental Authority in connection with the HSR Act filings, and shall provide the other Party with a reasonable opportunity to review and comment on any substantive written communications to any such Governmental Authority prior to submission.
**Section 6.05 Third-Party Consents**

Seller shall, and shall cause the Company to, use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain, as promptly as practicable following the date of this Agreement, all consents, waivers, approvals, authorizations, and notices required to be obtained or made in connection with the execution, delivery, and performance of this Agreement and the consummation of the transactions contemplated hereby, including those set forth on Schedule 4.05. Buyer shall use commercially reasonable efforts to cooperate with Seller and the Company in connection with obtaining such consents. Notwithstanding the foregoing, neither Seller nor the Company shall be required to pay or commit to pay any amount to (or incur any obligation in favor of) any Person from whom any such consent or waiver may be required (other than filing, application, or similar fees imposed by any Governmental Authority).

{"command":"cat > build_memo.py <<'PY'
from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Inches, Pt, RGBColor
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.enum.table import WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT, WD_CELL_VERTICAL_ALIGNMENT
from docx.enum.section import WD_SECTION
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.enum.style import WD_STYLE_TYPE
from docx.enum.text import WD_BREAK
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path('output/spa-markup-memorandum.docx')
OUT.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

def shade(cell, fill):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = tcPr.find(qn('w:shd'))
    if shd is None:
        shd = OxmlElement('w:shd'); tcPr.append(shd)
    shd.set(qn('w:fill'), fill)

def set_cell_text(cell, text, bold=False, color=None, size=9):
    cell.text = ''
    p = cell.paragraphs[0]
    r = p.add_run(text)
    r.bold = bold
    r.font.size = Pt(size)
    if color: r.font.color.rgb = RGBColor(*color)
    cell.vertical_alignment = WD_CELL_VERTICAL_ALIGNMENT.TOP

def set_repeat_table_header(row):
    trPr = row._tr.get_or_add_trPr()
    tblHeader = OxmlElement('w:tblHeader'); tblHeader.set(qn('w:val'), 'true'); trPr.append(tblHeader)

def add_page_number(paragraph):
    paragraph.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.RIGHT
    run = paragraph.add_run('Page ')
    fldChar1 = OxmlElement('w:fldChar'); fldChar1.set(qn('w:fldCharType'), 'begin')
    instrText = OxmlElement('w:instrText'); instrText.set(qn('xml:space'), 'preserve'); instrText.text = 'PAGE'
    fldChar2 = OxmlElement('w:fldChar'); fldChar2.set(qn('w:fldCharType'), 'end')
    run._r.append(fldChar1); run._r.append(instrText); run._r.append(fldChar2)

def add_para(doc, text='', style=None, bold=False, italic=False, color=None, size=None, align=None, space_after=4):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style=style)
    if text:
        r = p.add_run(text); r.bold=bold; r.italic=italic
        if color: r.font.color.rgb = RGBColor(*color)
        if size: r.font.size=Pt(size)
    if align is not None: p.alignment=align
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(space_after)
    return p

def add_bullets(doc, items, level=0):
    for item in items:
        p=doc.add_paragraph(style='List Bullet' if level==0 else 'List Bullet 2')
        p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2)
        p.add_run(item)

def add_numbered(doc, items):
    for item in items:
        p=doc.add_paragraph(style='List Number'); p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2); p.add_run(item)

def add_original(doc, text):
    p=doc.add_paragraph(); p.paragraph_format.left_indent=Inches(.2); p.paragraph_format.right_indent=Inches(.1)
    p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(5)
    r=p.add_run(text); r.font.name='Courier New'; r.font.size=Pt(8.5); r.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(128,0,0)
    return p

def add_proposed(doc, text):
    p=doc.add_paragraph(); p.paragraph_format.left_indent=Inches(.2); p.paragraph_format.right_indent=Inches(.1)
    p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(5)
    r=p.add_run(text); r.font.name='Courier New'; r.font.size=Pt(8.5); r.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(0,90,0)
    return p

def add_comment(doc, priority, text):
    p=doc.add_paragraph(); p.paragraph_format.left_indent=Inches(.2); p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(7)
    r=p.add_run(f'Track-changes comment — {priority}: '); r.bold=True; r.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(31,78,121)
    p.add_run(text)

def add_issue(doc, title, priority, original, proposed, comment, source=None):
    add_para(doc, title, style='Heading 3', bold=True)
    p=doc.add_paragraph(); p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2)
    r=p.add_run('Seller draft — original language'); r.bold=True; r.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(128,0,0)
    add_original(doc, original)
    p=doc.add_paragraph(); p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2)
    r=p.add_run('Buyer markup — proposed replacement / insertion'); r.bold=True; r.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(0,90,0)
    add_proposed(doc, proposed)
    add_comment(doc, priority, comment + (f' Source: {source}.' if source else ''))

def add_callout(doc, heading, body, fill='EAF2F8'):
    t=doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=1); t.alignment=WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER; t.autofit=True
    c=t.cell(0,0); shade(c,fill); c.text=''
    p=c.paragraphs[0]; p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2); rr=p.add_run(heading); rr.bold=True; rr.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(31,78,121)
    p=c.add_paragraph(body); p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2)
    doc.add_paragraph().paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(1)

# Document setup
doc=Document()
sec=doc.sections[0]
sec.top_margin=Inches(.65); sec.bottom_margin=Inches(.65); sec.left_margin=Inches(.78); sec.right_margin=Inches(.78)
styles=doc.styles
styles['Normal'].font.name='Arial'; styles['Normal'].font.size=Pt(9.5)
styles['Normal']._element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn('w:eastAsia'),'Arial')
for s in ['Heading 1','Heading 2','Heading 3']:
    styles[s].font.name='Arial'; styles[s]._element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn('w:eastAsia'),'Arial')
styles['Heading 1'].font.size=Pt(15); styles['Heading 1'].font.color.rgb=RGBColor(31,78,121)
styles['Heading 2'].font.size=Pt(12); styles['Heading 2'].font.color.rgb=RGBColor(31,78,121)
styles['Heading 3'].font.size=Pt(10.5); styles['Heading 3'].font.color.rgb=RGBColor(31,78,121)
# custom styles
for name, color in [('Small Gray', (100,100,100)),('Confidential',(128,0,0))]:
    st=styles.add_style(name, WD_STYLE_TYPE.PARAGRAPH); st.font.name='Arial'; st.font.size=Pt(8); st.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(*color)
# footer
footer=sec.footer
add_page_number(footer.paragraphs[0])

# Cover
p=doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER; p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(3)
r=p.add_run('ASHFORD, PENNINGTON & YATES LLP'); r.bold=True; r.font.size=Pt(14); r.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(31,78,121)
p=doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER; p.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(12)
r=p.add_run('PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT'); r.bold=True; r.font.size=Pt(10); r.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(128,0,0)
add_para(doc,'MARKUP MEMORANDUM',bold=True,size=18,align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER,space_after=4)
add_para(doc,'Seller’s Draft Stock Purchase Agreement',bold=True,size=13,align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER,space_after=16)
meta=doc.add_table(rows=5, cols=2); meta.alignment=WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER; meta.style='Table Grid'
meta_data=[('To','Elena Vasquez-Moreno, Partner, M&A Group\nJonathan Kreider, Senior Associate, M&A Group'),('From','Jonathan Kreider, Senior Associate, M&A Group'),('Date','October 29, 2025'),('Re','Acquisition of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC'),('Project','Project Cascade — Fund III platform acquisition')]
for i,(a,b) in enumerate(meta_data):

# Article I
add_para(doc,'I. ARTICLE I — DEFINITIONS',style='Heading 1')
add_issue(doc,'1. Material Adverse Effect — add disproportionate-impact qualifiers','CRITICAL',
'''“Material Adverse Effect” means any event, change, effect, development, state of facts, condition, circumstance, or occurrence that, individually or in the aggregate, has had or would reasonably be expected to have a material adverse effect on (a) the business, assets, liabilities, financial condition, or results of operations of the Company, or (b) the ability of Seller to consummate the transactions contemplated by this Agreement; provided, however, that none of the following ... shall be deemed to constitute ... a Material Adverse Effect: (i) changes in general economic ... conditions; (ii) changes in conditions generally affecting the environmental services industry; (iii) changes in Environmental Laws or regulations ...''',
'''Replace clauses (ii) and (iii) of the definition of “Material Adverse Effect” with the following (and retain the remainder of the definition as drafted):

“(ii) changes in conditions generally affecting the environmental services industry, except to the extent such changes disproportionately affect the Company relative to other participants in the environmental services industry; 

(iii) changes in Environmental Laws or regulations, except to the extent such changes disproportionately affect the Company relative to other participants in the environmental services industry;”''',
'''The target is itself an environmental-services business. A blanket carve-out for industry conditions and Environmental Law changes could exclude from the MAE analysis precisely the risks most relevant to the Company’s value and operating model. The qualifier is the firm’s non-negotiable Playbook position and preserves the customary industry-wide risk allocation while protecting Buyer from target-specific impact.''',
'Term Sheet §12 (MAE closing condition); Playbook §2.1; Partner Instructions ¶1')

add_issue(doc,'2. Indemnification Cap definition — conform to executed Term Sheet','HIGH',
'''“Indemnification Cap” means Forty-Three Million Dollars ($43,000,000), which is equal to twenty percent (20%) of the Base Enterprise Value.''',
'''“Indemnification Cap” means Twenty-Six Million Eight Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars ($26,875,000), which is equal to twelve and one-half percent (12.5%) of the Base Enterprise Value.''',
'''The seller draft deviates from an express, binding economic term. The agreed cap is 12.5% × $215,000,000 = $26,875,000; the proposed $43,000,000 cap is 20% and is not a drafting discretion point. The R&W policy does not justify reducing or changing the SPA cap structure; the SPA must conform to the Term Sheet.''',
'Term Sheet §8 (General Indemnification Cap); Term Sheet §18(iv); Playbook §§5.1 and 14')

# Article II
add_para(doc,'II. ARTICLE II — PURCHASE PRICE AND EARNOUT',style='Heading 1')
add_issue(doc,'3. Section 2.05(d) — delete affirmative earnout operating covenants','CRITICAL',
'''From and after the Closing Date through the end of the Earnout Period, Buyer shall, and shall cause the Company to, operate the business of the Company in a manner consistent with past practice and in good faith to maximize the Earnout Payment. Without limiting the foregoing, Buyer shall not, and shall cause the Company not to, take any action that would reasonably be expected to reduce the Adjusted EBITDA of the Company below the levels that would otherwise have been achieved. In furtherance of the foregoing, during the Earnout Period, Buyer shall cause the Company to maintain substantially the same level of personnel, equipment, and other resources as in effect immediately prior to the Closing Date and shall not divert or redirect any contracts, customers, revenues, or business opportunities of the Company to Buyer or any of its Affiliates.''',
'''Replace Section 2.05(d) in its entirety with:

“(d) Operation of the Business During the Earnout Period. Following the Closing, Buyer shall not, and shall cause the Company not to, take any action with the primary purpose of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment. For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this Section 2.05(d) shall restrict Buyer’s right to operate, integrate, restructure, or otherwise manage the Company and its business in Buyer’s sole discretion, including the right to make capital expenditure decisions, change pricing, make personnel decisions, enter new markets, make strategic investments, acquire or dispose of businesses or assets, reorganize the Company or its business, allocate corporate overhead, and make other operational modifications. No such action shall constitute a breach of this Section 2.05(d) unless taken with the primary purpose of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment. Buyer shall have no obligation to maintain the Company as a separate entity, maintain any particular level of capital expenditures, retain any particular employees, or operate the Company in accordance with past practice.”''',
'''The proposed covenant would handcuff Buyer’s platform integration and operational judgment through December 31, 2026, and create litigation exposure over ordinary-course decisions. The Term Sheet expressly requires only the narrow “primary purpose” negative covenant and disclaims affirmative operating obligations. The proposed replacement preserves a bad-faith manipulation protection without requiring Buyer to maximize an earnout or maintain the pre-Closing business model.''',
'Term Sheet §5 (Earnout Covenant); Playbook §7.2; Partner Instructions ¶3')

add_issue(doc,'4. Adjusted EBITDA — prevent post-Closing accounting and allocation disputes','HIGH',
'''“Adjusted EBITDA” means ... net income ... plus interest expense, income tax expense, and depreciation and amortization ... and further adjusted to exclude (i) non-recurring transaction costs ... (ii) purchase-price accounting adjustments ... (iii) extraordinary or non-recurring items, and (iv) management fees, monitoring fees, or similar fees charged by Buyer or any of its Affiliates ... as determined in accordance with GAAP applied consistently with the Company’s past practice.''',
'''Replace the definition of “Adjusted EBITDA” with:

“Adjusted EBITDA” means, for the applicable Measurement Period, the Company’s net income determined in accordance with GAAP, consistently applied, plus interest expense, income tax expense, and depreciation and amortization, in each case to the extent deducted in determining net income, and adjusted to exclude or add back, without duplication: (a) transaction-related costs and expenses incurred in connection with the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, including legal, accounting, advisory, financing, insurance underwriting, and other professional fees; (b) purchase accounting adjustments arising from the transactions contemplated hereby; (c) Buyer-directed integration costs, restructuring charges, and other costs incurred at the direction of Buyer or its Affiliates in connection with integrating, reorganizing, or restructuring the Company or its business; (d) non-recurring items, including one-time litigation costs, regulatory penalties, extraordinary items, and gains or losses not arising in the ordinary course; (e) corporate overhead or other allocations imposed by Buyer or its Affiliates to the extent not charged to the Company on a consistent basis before the Closing; (f) intercompany charges, management fees, monitoring fees, or similar charges imposed by Buyer or its Affiliates, except to the extent expressly approved in writing by Seller; and (g) the $1,600,000 annual Affiliate Lease rent to the extent the amount exceeds fair market rent or is not incurred on arm’s-length terms. Adjusted EBITDA shall be calculated consistently with this Agreement and the detailed methodology in Exhibit D; provided that this definition and Exhibit D shall control over any inconsistent historical practice.”''',
'''The current definition includes some agreed exclusions but does not expressly address Buyer-directed integration/restructuring costs, unhistorical corporate allocations, intercompany charges, or the disclosed $1.6M affiliate lease. A precise definition is required to implement the Term Sheet and the Playbook’s anti-manipulation guidance while preserving Buyer’s operating flexibility. The affiliate-lease add-back should be confirmed against the final fair-market-rent analysis before signing.''',
'Term Sheet §5 (Adjusted EBITDA); Playbook §7.1; DD Memo §VIII (Additional Recommendations); Schedule 4.21')

add_issue(doc,'5. Section 4.15 — strengthen environmental permit and insurance representations','HIGH',
'''(b) The Company holds all Environmental Permits necessary for the conduct of its business as currently conducted, and all such Environmental Permits are in full force and effect. Schedule 4.15(b) sets forth ... twenty-three (23) active Environmental Permits ... The Company is in compliance in all material respects ... No Action is pending or, to the Knowledge of the Company, threatened to revoke, suspend, cancel, terminate, modify, or not renew any Environmental Permit.

(f) The Company maintains environmental impairment liability insurance ... $15,000,000 aggregate / $5,000,000 per occurrence ... and project-specific environmental liability insurance relating to Hargrove ... $10,000,000.''',
'''Replace Sections 4.15(b) and 4.15(f) with:

“(b) Environmental Permits. The Company holds each of the twenty-three (23) Environmental Permits listed on Schedule 4.15(b), and such Environmental Permits constitute all material Environmental Permits necessary for the conduct of the Company’s business as currently conducted. Each Environmental Permit is valid, in full force and effect, and in good standing. The Company is in compliance in all material respects with each Environmental Permit. No Environmental Permit is subject to any pending or, to the Knowledge of the Company, threatened revocation, suspension, cancellation, termination, modification, non-renewal, or material restriction. No fact or circumstance exists that would reasonably be expected to result in any such action. Except as set forth on Schedule 4.15(b), no notice, consent, approval, filing, or other action is required from any Governmental Authority in connection with a change of control of the Company or its Environmental Permits, and Schedule 4.15(b) identifies each such requirement.”

“(f) Environmental Insurance. The environmental impairment liability policy and the Hargrove Industrial Site project-specific environmental liability policy listed on Schedule 4.17 are in full force and effect, all premiums due have been paid, and the Company has not received written notice of cancellation, non-renewal, reservation of rights, or material modification. No insurer has denied or disputed coverage for any material environmental claim, except as disclosed on Schedule 4.15(f).”''',
'''The seller draft confirms current permits and policy limits but does not address change-of-control requirements, permit good standing, or facts that could lead to revocation/suspension. The DD Memo identifies 23 permits across OR, WA, CA and NV and specifically warns that state agencies may require notification or approval even in a stock deal. The insurance language should also capture the absence of cancellation/non-renewal/coverage defenses for the Hargrove project and general EIL program.''',
'Playbook §§12.1 and 13.2; DD Memo §§V and VII; Schedule 4.15(b), Schedule 4.17')

add_issue(doc,'6. Section 4.16 — add termination, novation and ownership-change representations','CRITICAL',
'''(a) The Company is a party to four (4) active government contracts ...
(b) Each Government Contract is in full force and effect ... The Company is not in material breach or default ...
(c) Neither the Company nor any of its directors, officers, or employees is subject to debarment ...
(d) The Company has complied in all material respects with all applicable procurement Laws ...''',
'''Add the following as new Sections 4.16(e) through (h):

“(e) No Government Contract is subject to any pending or, to the Knowledge of the Company, threatened termination for default or convenience, suspension, non-renewal, material modification, cure notice, show-cause notice, or adverse audit finding. No Governmental Authority or contracting officer has notified the Company of an intent to terminate, suspend, not renew, or materially modify any Government Contract.

(f) The execution, delivery, and performance of this Agreement and the consummation of the transactions contemplated hereby do not, and will not, violate any Government Contract or applicable procurement Law, except for any notice, consent, approval, novation, recognition agreement, or other filing identified on Schedule 4.16.

(g) The Company has identified on Schedule 4.16 each Government Contract for which a change in ownership or control requires notice to, consent or approval of, or a novation or recognition agreement with, the applicable Governmental Authority or contracting officer, including the contracts with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the Bureau of Land Management. The Company has not received any denial or written indication that any such novation, recognition, consent, or approval will not be granted.
